newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ENGLISH F.A. AIM TO SETTLE INJURY CLAIMS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLISH F.A. AIM TO SETTLE INJURY CLAIMS.

text.p: The English F.A. want to introduce a no-fault compensation scheme in soccer after a former player was awarded 250,000 pounds ($410,000) in damages on Thursday for a tackle which ended his career.
Brian McCord, who played for English second division club Stockport, had sued for compensation after Swansea captain John Cornforth badly damaged his right leg in a game in 1993.

F.A. director of public affairs David Davies said: "Everybody has the right to take legal action but the benefit of a no-fault compensation scheme within the game -- and supported by all parts of it -- appears to be clear.
He said the F.A. would discuss the issue with the premier league, Football League and Professional Footballers' Association (PFA).

"Our sympathies lie with all players who find themselves caught in the legal system in this way," said Davies. "Of course, it's a problem that is increasingly faced by other sports as well as our own.
"But football isn't and shouldn't be outside the civil and criminal laws of the land."
McCord's solicitor said the damages decision was a landmark because there was no system for players to obtain compensation for injuries received during games.
"I believe it is time for the sporting bodies to devise some system of compensation without redress to the courts," he said.
The judge said Cornforth had not taken reasonable care when making the tackle.
PFA chief executive Gordon Taylor reassured his members that they had nothing to fear from the courts as long as they remained within the boundaries of acceptable behaviour on the pitch.
"It sends a warning to players that the pitch is not an oasis that is outside the law of the land."
Taylor said it was wrong for players to believe it was possible to hide behind an insurance policy when they go on to the field of play.
"No insurance company in the world is going to issue a policy which allows someone to step outside the law."
